Where Prussia Fought

Every named land and sea battle fought by Brandenburg-Prussia, from the Thirty Years' War to the founding of the German Empire in 1871: where each was fought, against whom, who won, how large a part the Prussians played, and how sure we can be.

The map, period by period

Pick a period, or drag the year slider to see the battles of any ten years; Play runs through them from 1618. Each dot is a place, its area the number of battles there, and its slices the opponents, starting at 12 o'clock and running clockwise in the order of the legend; grey is civil. Diamonds are sea battles; dashed rings are battles placed only within their region; triangles at the edge point to battles off the map (Cape St. Vincent, Toulon, Arguin, the Rif and Havana). Nearby dots merge as you zoom out and split as you zoom in. Hover or tap a dot for its battles; select it to list them with their full records.

Wins, draws and losses

The Prussian record in the 504 battles that Prussia fought as principal or as a major ally and whose result is known. Not scored: the 61 battles in which only a small Prussian contingent fought (13 of them, in 1870–71, by South German troops alone), the 16 with unknown results and the 3 civil battles. Each battle counts once in its opponent group and once in the total; among the main opponents it counts against each principal enemy. Select a row to list its battles.

Brandenburg-Prussia: 1618–1700; the Kingdom of Prussia: 1701–1866; the North German Confederation: 1867–71, with its South German allies. Frederick II in person: the 31 battles at which the king commanded on the field. Counted, with a flag: Schill's raid of 1809, made without orders, and the corps that fought for Napoleon in 1812.

All the battles

Select a row for the full record: date, place, sides and allies, commanders, the Prussian force, strengths and losses, the sources, and every doubt and flag. Results give the winner first; the coloured edge marks a Prussian win (blue), draw (grey) or defeat (orange); no edge: not scored. Borderline marks an entry that may not meet the rules, kept with the reason; not scored a battle of a small Prussian contingent, with an unknown result, or civil; Schill and for Napoleon the flagged battles of 1809 and 1812 (hover a label to read why). A hollow marker means that only the region of the battle is known.

How it was made

What counts as a battle

A named land or sea battle, combat (Gefecht) or siege with real fighting in which a Brandenburg-Prussian force fought: one with its own name in English or German Wikipedia's battle articles, lists and campaign boxes, or in the standard works. Sieges count when there was real fighting (assaults, sorties, relief battles); a distinctly named battle inside a siege is its own entry. Left out: unnamed skirmishes and outpost affairs, marches, bombardments without an engagement, and fortresses that surrendered without a siege. When in doubt an entry is kept and marked borderline, with the reason: 248 entries, most of them minor actions known from one source, short sieges that were mostly blockades, or battles in which the Prussian part is uncertain.

Who counts as Prussia

The state of the Hohenzollerns from the union of Brandenburg with the Duchy of Prussia (1618) to 1871: Brandenburg-Prussia under the electors (to 1700; in the list, the Brandenburgers), the Kingdom of Prussia (1701–1866), and the North German Confederation (1867–71), whose army was the Prussian army enlarged with the North German contingents. In 1870–71 it fought with its South German allies; the list calls that side the Germans. A battle is in if a Prussian force fought as the principal belligerent, or as a major ally: a substantial, distinct force in a coalition army, as at Blenheim, Turin, Leipzig and Waterloo.

Contingents

61 battles in which only a small Prussian contingent fought, in an army led by others, are mapped and listed but not scored: Brandenburg troops in Dutch and allied armies in the 1670s–1710s, a few squadrons with Ferdinand of Brunswick, Blücher's command at Brienne and Craonne without Prussian units engaged, the North German federal corps of 1815. So are 13 actions of 1870–71 fought by South German troops alone under Prussian supreme command. Scored, they would add 37–3–21 (won-drawn-lost).

Schill, 1809, and the corps of 1812

Two groups are counted, and flagged. In April–May 1809 Major Ferdinand von Schill took his hussar regiment to war against Napoleon and his German allies without orders, and the king disowned him; his four battles (Dodendorf, Dömitz, Damgarten, Stralsund) were fought by Prussian troops under a Prussian officer, so they are counted and scored (1–1–2). In 1812 the Prussian auxiliary corps fought for Napoleon, as his ally, against the Russians in Courland (Ekau, Riga, Dahlenkirchen, Mesoten); these are counted and scored too (2–0–2), until Yorck took the corps out of the war at Tauroggen on 30 December 1812.

Civil battles

Prussian troops against Prussian insurgents, 3 in all (Berlin in March 1848, Elberfeld and Iserlohn in May 1849), are mapped and listed, in grey, but not scored. The rising of 1848 in the Prussian province of Posen is counted against Polish insurgents, and the Prussian interventions in Saxony, Baden and the Palatinate in 1849 against German revolutionaries.

Colours and dots

Each battle takes the colour of its opponent group: French, Austrians and the Empire, Swedes and Danes, Poles, Russians, other Germans, and others; grey for civil. Each place is drawn as a small pie: its area grows with the number of battles there, and the slices give the number against each opponent. The seven colours are checked for colour-blind readers and in dark mode.

Wins, draws and losses

The victor is the side that held the field, routed the enemy, took the place or destroyed the fleet; strategic results and disagreements between the sources are in the notes. In a siege the besieger wins if the place fell, and the defender if the siege was raised. A draw is an indecisive battle, or one that both sides claimed with no clear verdict from modern scholarship. 16 battles whose result the sources consulted do not give are listed, marked, and not scored.

Research

Twenty research batches by period, each following the same written rules and citing its sources battle by battle; then a check against every battle in German Wikipedia's category of Prussian battles and the battle categories of each war in English and German, which added 9 battles, corrected 19 entries and removed 4 (listed under Left out); then checks of names, of possible doubles, and of every position against the present-day country. Positions: 389 known, 184 approximate, 11 only within their region.

What may be missing

Minor actions known only from regimental histories, the Kronoskaf narratives of the Seven Years' War and the General Staff histories of 1741–62 and 1813–14 may still be missing; 5 candidates whose pages could not be read are listed under Left out, with the reason.

The images

The 10 images were made for X in the house style of the series, 3200 × 1800 pixels: the overview map with the number of battles per five years; Germany, Poland and the Baltic with Pomerania; Brandenburg, Saxony, Silesia and Bohemia; France and the Low Countries with Paris and Metz; the win-draw-loss tables; and the list in five parts.

Data

Every battle with its date, war, place, coordinates, sides, allies, commanders, result, the Prussian state and role, the Prussian force, strengths and losses, flags and doubts, sources and notes: as a CSV table, as JSON, or as a spreadsheet with the record tables and the entries left out; and the record alone as CSV.

Battles (.csv)Data (.json)Spreadsheet (.xlsx)Record (.csv)

Sources, cited battle by battle: above all the battle, war and campaign articles and categories of English and German Wikipedia, with French Wikipedia for 1870–71 and Polish Wikipedia for 1794 and 1848; Howard's history of the Franco-Prussian War, Duffy on Frederick's army, Wawro, Petre, Nafziger and Bodart; historyofwar.org, napoleon-empire.org and the Kronoskaf project on the Seven Years' War; and, for minor actions, regimental histories and the Allgemeine Deutsche Biographie. Map: Natural Earth; today's borders dashed.

Calls made

Where the rules left room for judgement, this is how it was settled. The map, the record and the list follow the call shown; the alternative is given so that readers can weigh it.

Left out

Where Prussia Fought: battles of Prussia, 1618–1871. Compiled October 2026. Each record keeps its sources and a note on anything disputed. The companion sets: Where the Romans Fought, 753 BCE – 1475 CE, Where the Greeks Fought, c. 700 BCE – c. 10 CE and Where the Greeks Fought, 1461 to Today.
